title: the rains
hook: Rama's monsoon poem: a sky that carried the sea for nine months

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sugriva crowned, and Rama waiting out the monsoon in the cave on Prasravana.

The smell of wet earth after months of dust. The sky changing color in an afternoon. The whole land seeming to breathe out. Rama, waiting in the cave, describes the monsoon to Lakshmana, and it's some of the most famous nature writing in Sanskrit: a long, beautiful, aching poem. Rama sees all of that, and something else too.
screen: `THE SMELL OF WET EARTH.` → `FAMOUS NATURE WRITING.` → `RAMA SEES SOMETHING ELSE TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's how Valmiki's Rama sees it. The sky, he says, drank the waters of the sea through the sun's rays, carried them for nine months, and now is giving birth to rain: the monsoon as a long pregnancy, finally delivered. He sees clouds piled like mountains and mountains wrapped in clouds. He hears peacocks crying out and sees them dancing. Frogs wake and call after the long dry months. Rivers swell and rush toward the sea. And yet the rain that is lovely for everyone is painful for him. Travelers are heading home, he says. Kings have stopped their campaigns. Everyone is going back to the one they love, and he can't. So every lovely thing he sees, he sees as someone separated from Sita. In Sanskrit poetry that feeling has a name, viraha, love in separation, and Rama in the rains became one of its great examples. Poets for centuries after wrote monsoon verses in the same key: someone far from the one they love, clouds overhead, and the rain saying what they can't. The poem does something for Rama, too, not only for us. Describing the rain carefully slows him down. He isn't raging, and he isn't collapsing. He's looking. Lakshmana listens. And four months, one cloud at a time, begin to pass.
screen: `THE SKY CARRIED THE SEA.` · `PEACOCKS, FROGS, SWOLLEN RIVERS.` · `VIRAHA: LOVE IN SEPARATION.` · `LOOKING SLOWS HIM DOWN.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing in front of you or out the window, and describe it to yourself slowly, the way Rama described the rain: its color, its edges, the light on it, what it reminds you of. Breathe between each detail. If your mind drifts to someone you're missing, let that be part of the looking too, then come back.
The rains. Rama's monsoon poem: a sky carrying the sea for nine months, and every lovely thing seen through missing Sita.
Your line: looking slows him down. Even longing can be held with care. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The monsoon is woven into Hindu poetry, music and festival life; Rama's description in the Kishkindha Kanda is often cited as an early model for the monsoon poems of later Sanskrit and Indian literature.

chat.says: Rama's monsoon poem sounds lovely. Why is it sad too?
options: Everyone is going home to the one they love, and he cannot; he is missing Sita.
The rains flooded their cave, and he was afraid they would drown there.

chat.meaning: Rama's rain poem is viraha, love in separation: travelers and kings head home, and every lovely thing reminds him he's apart from Sita.

viraha.meaning: love in separation: longing for someone far away

Sita.meaning: Rama's wife, carried off by Ravana

Lakshmana.meaning: Rama's younger brother, beside him in exile
